items.title: FinCEN & OFAC propose GENIUS Act AML/sanctions rules for stablecoin issuers
items.summary: On 8 Apr 2026 FinCEN and OFAC issued a joint NPRM implementing the GENIUS Act: permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) would be treated as BSA 'financial institutions', must run AML/CFT programmes and — for the first time — maintain an explicit sanctions-compliance programme. Final rules take effect 12 months after issuance.
items.soWhat: Stablecoin issuers become regulated FIs with their own sanctions duties — counterparty risk on compliant issuers falls, but expect them to wield freeze/seize powers; align issuer-freeze playbooks now.

sources.name: Federal Register — PPSI AML/sanctions NPRM
Mayer Brown — Stable rules for stablecoins

items.title: FATF: stablecoins now 84% of illicit crypto volume; wants issuer freeze/burn controls
items.summary: FATF's 3 Mar 2026 targeted report flags stablecoin misuse via P2P transfers and unhosted wallets; Chainalysis puts stablecoins at 84% of illicit virtual-asset volume in 2025. FATF urges issuers to be able to freeze, burn or withdraw in the secondary market and to fully implement Recommendation 15.
items.soWhat: The 84% figure reframes stablecoins as the primary laundering rail — make issuer freeze capability a weighted criterion in vendor and counterparty assessment, and prioritise stablecoin-flow tracing.

items.soWhat: Bank-regulator reinforcement: stablecoin issuance is converging on bank-grade AML expectations across multiple US supervisors — treat compliant issuers more like regulated counterparties.

items.title: Treasury pushes 'programmable' on-protocol sanctions enforcement
items.summary: Treasury (FinCEN/OFAC) proposals would have digital-asset firms build systems where sanctions enforcement, transaction blocking and monitoring are automatic and embedded in the protocol — compliance continuous and built-in rather than after-the-fact.

items.title: EU 20th sanctions package bans all transactions with Russian and Belarusian CASPs
items.summary: Adopted 23 April 2026 and effective 24 May 2026, the EU's 20th Russia sanctions package moves beyond entity-level listing: it bans any EU person from transacting with any crypto-asset service provider established in Russia or Belarus. Four Russian-linked crypto assets are simultaneously prohibited — A7A5, RUBx, and both the Russian and Belarusian digital rubles. Decentralised platforms established in Russia are explicitly in scope.
items.soWhat: Sector-level bans are structurally harder to route around than entity lists — a new Russian exchange is in scope from day one without waiting for a specific listing. Review all counterparty flows for Russian/Belarusian CASP involvement and treat the A7A5, RUBx and digital ruble prohibitions as screening inputs on par with SDN entries.

items.title: UK OFSI designates HTX (Huobi), EXMO and A7A5 stablecoin issuer — first Regulation 17A action against crypto exchanges
items.summary: On 26 May 2026 the UK FCDO designated 18 entities under its Russia sanctions regime, including Huobi/HTX ($3.3tn 2025 trading volume), EXMO, BitPapa, and A7 Guarantee — the entity behind the A7A5 ruble stablecoin. This is the first UK application of Regulation 17A to crypto exchanges, prohibiting UK financial institutions from acting as correspondent banks or processing payments for any of the 18 entities. Major exchanges began increasing transfer scrutiny with HTX within 24 hours.
items.soWhat: HTX's scale means many institutions will have indirect exposure via omnibus accounts or liquidity routing — run an immediate lookback for HTX/EXMO/BitPapa counterparty flows and update screening lists. Regulation 17A's correspondent-bank prohibition extends to payment processing, so the exposure surface is wider than wallet screening alone.

items.title: Chinese-language money laundering networks: $16.1B in 2025 via full-service laundering-as-a-service
items.summary: Chainalysis's 2026 Crypto Crime Report identified Chinese-language money laundering networks (CLMNs) as the dominant professional laundering infrastructure in crypto, moving $16.1 billion in 2025 (~$44M/day across 1,799+ active wallets) — roughly 20% of all known illicit crypto volume. CLMNs run six discrete service lines via Telegram: point brokers, money mules, OTC desks, 'Black U' USDT services, gambling cash-outs, and money-movement services. OFAC subsequently designated the Prince Group; FinCEN designated Huione Group under Section 311.
items.soWhat: CLMNs act as the shared back-office for DPRK heists, pig-butchering proceeds, and ransomware — meaning seemingly unrelated illicit events converge through the same wallet clusters. Cross-entity cluster analytics (not just direct attribution) is the only reliable detection method; add Telegram-advertised service wallets to your screening feed.

typology.vector: Chinese-language money laundering networks (CLMN) — full-service laundering-as-a-service via Telegram
controls: Cross-entity cluster analytics (not direct attribution alone)
OTC desk and 'Black U' USDT flow detection
obligations: SAR on DPRK-nexus and scam-proceeds flows
OFAC / UN screening of CLMN-linked wallet clusters

items.title: AMLA launches direct-supervision selection: NCAs submit data by 15 Aug 2026, provisional list Sep 2026
items.summary: EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) has published the reporting package for national competent authorities to identify obliged entities eligible for AMLA's direct supervision from 2028. NCAs must submit data by 15 August 2026; a provisional list of ~40 high-risk cross-border firms — including large CASPs — is expected by end-September 2026. AMLA's Single Rulebook applies across all 27 member states from 10 July 2027.
items.soWhat: Any EU-facing bank or large CASP with material cross-border AML exposure should treat AMLA readiness as a live project now: the 26 regulatory technical standards and guidelines AMLA is releasing in 2026–Q1 2027 define what 'adequate' looks like, and the August 15 NCA data-submission deadline means the selection criteria are being applied to live data right now.

items.title: OFAC designates Nobitex and three Iranian crypto exchanges for IRGC ties and sanctions evasion
items.summary: On 2 June 2026, OFAC designated Nobitex — Iran's largest crypto exchange handling over 50% of Iranian digital-asset inflows — alongside Wallex, Bitpin, and Ramzinex, and four named executives. Nobitex processed hundreds of millions in stablecoins for the Central Bank of Iran, handled transactions for IRGC-affiliated ransomware actors, and enabled regime insiders to move wealth during internet blackouts. The action is the third enforcement layer in five months targeting Iran's domestic crypto ecosystem, following the April CBI wallet freeze.
items.soWhat: Four domestic Iranian exchanges are now fully off-limits; any correspondent-banking or payment-processing exposure — even indirect via omnibus accounts — triggers sanctions risk. Screen for Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, and Ramzinex counterparty flows immediately and review IRGC-linked cluster addresses newly added to the SDN list. Chainalysis estimates IRGC-linked addresses account for over 50% of total value received by the Iranian crypto ecosystem in Q4 2025 — meaning Iran-nexus exposure is likely underestimated without cluster analytics.

items.title: MiCA transitional period ends 1 July 2026 — ESMA orders unlicensed CASPs to cease EU services
items.summary: ESMA's April 2026 statement confirmed the hard cutoff: after 1 July 2026, any entity providing crypto-asset services to EU clients without a MiCA authorisation is in breach of EU law and must immediately cease operations. Unlicensed CASPs must have 'immediately executable' wind-down plans and must off-board clients to authorised platforms. ESMA explicitly rejected paper-only plans and put NCAs on notice to enforce. Penalties reach up to 12.5% of global annual turnover alongside cease-and-desist orders and executive liability.
items.soWhat: The enforcement window is now 26 days away. For licensed banks the practical risk is counterparty exposure: a CASP that quietly continues operating post-deadline becomes an unlicensed counterparty overnight, with all the associated AML and reputational risk. Conduct a pre-July sweep of CASP counterparty authorisation status — any that are not MiCA-licensed by July 1 should be flagged for relationship review.

items.title: Pig-butchering 2026: agentic AI grooming, approval-phishing drains, and Southeast Asia scam-centre strikes
items.summary: Pig-butchering has industrialised in 2026. Criminal syndicates now deploy agentic AI to run thousands of simultaneous grooming relationships, pushing average scam payouts up 253% year-on-year (from $782 to $2,764 per transaction). The attack endgame has shifted to 'approval phishing' — victims are manipulated into signing wallet-spending permissions that attackers drain weeks later, bypassing conventional 'send crypto' red flags. In April 2026, DOJ, OFAC, and State launched a coordinated multi-pronged strike against Southeast Asian scam centres; Operation Atlantic (March 2026) targeted approval-phishing victims alongside UK NCA and Canadian authorities.
items.soWhat: AI-enabled scale means scam-proceeds volumes will keep rising even as individual victim counts plateau — expect higher-value SARs from investment-fraud flows. Approval-phishing bypasses typical transaction monitoring; update typologies to flag repeated ERC-20 token-approval contract interactions from retail wallets. Downstream laundering flows through Chinese-language money laundering networks (see feed-chinese-mln-laas-typology), so pig-butchering proceeds and CLMN cluster screening should be treated as coupled intelligence.

typology.vector: AI-enhanced pig-butchering via agentic grooming and approval-phishing wallet drains
controls: Token-approval contract interaction monitoring for retail customers
Higher-value SAR triggers on investment-fraud proceeds
Screening of Southeast Asian scam-centre wallet clusters

obligations: SAR on suspected investment fraud proceeds

items.title: FCA leads first UK crackdown on illegal peer-to-peer crypto trading — eight sites raided
items.summary: On 22 April 2026, the FCA (working with HMRC and the South West Regional Organised Crime Unit) raided eight premises suspected of running unlicensed peer-to-peer crypto exchange businesses, issuing cease-and-desist letters at each site. It is the first FCA enforcement action against illegal P2P crypto trading. Evidence gathered is supporting ongoing criminal investigations. No FCA-registered P2P crypto businesses currently operate in the UK.
items.soWhat: The FCA is not waiting for October 2027's full crypto regime to enforce against unlicensed activity. UK banks should scrutinise the registration status of crypto counterparties now — any P2P business without FCA registration is already illegal, carrying live AML and reputational exposure. The action also signals heightened pre-authorisation scrutiny: firms preparing September 2026 licence applications will face a regulator that has already demonstrated willingness to act.

items.title: DOJ probes Binance for $1.7B in Iran and Russia flows; senators challenge monitorship effectiveness
items.summary: On 11 March 2026, the DOJ launched an investigation into over $1 billion in flows through Binance to Iran-linked entities — transactions that Binance's own internal compliance team had flagged before at least five investigators were fired in late 2025. Fortune's reporting identified $1.7 billion in flows linked to Iran proxies and Russia's shadow fleet. By April-May 2026, senators Blumenthal, Warren, Van Hollen, and Gallego sent formal letters to DOJ and FinCEN questioning the effectiveness of Binance's court-ordered compliance monitorship (established under its 2023 $4.3B settlement).
items.soWhat: Even a post-settlement, court-monitored exchange can carry material sanctions exposure — the monitorship is not a blanket counterparty assurance. Banks with Binance exposure (including via omnibus accounts, liquidity routing, or payment rails) should run a lookback for Iran-nexus transactions and reassess whether the monitorship constitutes a sufficient control for continued counterparty status. The whistleblower-firing detail creates added reputational risk in any regulatory examination.

items.title: Treasury GENIUS Act tech report: AI-powered crypto oversight and a proposed 'digital-asset hold law'
items.summary: On 6 March 2026, Treasury published its congressionally-mandated report on innovative technologies to counter illicit finance in digital assets under the GENIUS Act. The report endorses AI, digital identity, blockchain analytics, and APIs as priority compliance tools, and proposes a legislative 'digital-asset hold law' safe harbour — allowing financial institutions to temporarily freeze suspicious crypto transactions without liability while investigations proceed. Treasury also signalled a nuanced shift on mixers, acknowledging legitimate privacy use cases rather than treating all mixer-touched funds as presumptively illicit.
items.soWhat: The proposed hold-law safe harbour removes a key legal barrier for proactive crypto intervention, directly reinforcing the on-ledger enforcement thesis already in Treasury's NPRM (see feed-treasury-programmable-enforcement). For bank compliance teams, the report is also a forward indicator for supervisory expectations: AI-assisted transaction monitoring and blockchain analytics are being positioned as required capabilities, not differentiators. The mixer nuance matters too — blanket mixer-flag policies may need recalibration against a mixed-use risk-based standard.

items.title: Ransomware laundering pivots from mixers to cross-chain bridges: 66% bridge surge, 37% mixer decline
items.summary: TRM Labs' 2026 Crypto Crime Report documents a sharp behavioural shift in ransomware post-payment laundering across 2024-25: bridge-related activity grew 66% while mixer use fell 37%, as threat actors adapted to OFAC sanctions against Tornado Cash and heightened mixer monitoring. Ransomware itself is growing — 93 new variants emerged (a 94% jump) and $820M in payments were recorded in 2025. Cross-chain bridges offer routing flexibility and liquidity-venue diversity that is structurally harder to trace via wallet-level blockchain analytics.
items.soWhat: Detection rules anchored to mixer-flag typologies are increasingly stale for ransomware proceeds. Update transaction monitoring to flag multi-hop cross-chain bridge sequences — particularly patterns that hop tokens across chains before converging on an exchange deposit address. The 94% jump in active ransomware strains also means the incoming volume of laundering flows to the financial system is growing; expect higher SAR volumes from this vector.

typology.vector: Ransomware post-payment laundering via cross-chain bridges (displacing mixers)
controls: Multi-hop cross-chain bridge interaction monitoring for unusual routing patterns
Rapid screening of newly-emerging ransomware strain payment addresses
Expanding mixer-only detection rules to cover cross-chain routing signatures
obligations: SAR on suspected ransomware payment proceeds
OFAC screening of designated ransomware operator address clusters
